--- title: "Capacity Expansion" subtitle: "Lecture 16" author: "Vivek Srikrishnan" course: "BEE 4750" institution: "Cornell University" date: "November 2, 2026" format: revealjs: slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all center-title-slide: true width: 1280 height: 720 transition: none toc: true toc-depth: 1 toc-title: "Overview" history: false link-external-newwindow: true theme: ../sass/slides.scss template-partials: - title-slide.html menu: numbers: true html-math-method: mathjax include-in-header: mathjax-config.html date-format: long email-obfuscation: javascript chalkboard: theme: whiteboard buttons: true controls: true engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11.5"] execute: freeze: auto daemon: 600 --- # Review of Last Class ## Economic Dispatch - Dispatch runs the plants we **already have** at least cost. Minimum outputs, ramping, and transmission constraints can break the merit order. - The price of electricity is the demand constraint's **shadow price**: the cost of serving one more MWh. **Raises the question**: what should we **build**? ::: {.notes} Ask whether anything about economic dispatch was unclear, especially the sign of the shadow price (relaxing demand means serving one less MWh, so JuMP reports a negative number). ::: ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # The Capacity Expansion Problem ## Capacity Expansion **Capacity expansion**: which generating resources to build, and how much, to meet future demand (*load*). - Typical objective: minimize cost. - Other goals may enter as constraints: reducing CO~2~ emissions, fuel diversity, reliability. We'll look at a **greenfield** problem (no existing plants), not a **brownfield** one (adding to an existing fleet). ::: {.notes} Capacity expansion sits at the long end of the decision time scales: years, not hours. The dispatch decision is nested inside it: whatever we build has to be run every hour, and the running costs are part of the case for building it. Most real planning is brownfield, adding to a fleet that is already there. ::: ## Plant Types - natural gas: **combined cycle** (CCGT) or **combustion turbines** (CT); - coal and nuclear; - renewables: wind, solar, hydro, geothermal. They differ in **fixed cost** (to build) and **variable cost** (to run). ::: {.notes} Cheap-to-build plants that are expensive to run (CTs) suit loads that occur only a few hours a year; expensive-to-build plants that are cheap to run suit loads that are there all year. ::: ## Generator and Demand Data ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} gens = DataFrame(CSV.File("data/capacity_expansion/generators.csv")) n_types = 4 # the thermal types: nuclear, coal, CCGT and CT gas_price = 7.21 # delivered to U.S. power plants in 2022 [$/MMBtu] coal_price = 2.36 # Variable cost of each plant type [$/MWh, to the dollar] at given fuel prices: # the fuel burned per MWh times its price, plus other running costs function variable_costs(gas, coal) costs = zeros(Int, nrow(gens)) for g in 1:nrow(gens) fuel_price = 0 if gens[g, :Fuel] == "Gas" fuel_price = gas elseif gens[g, :Fuel] == "Coal" fuel_price = coal end costs[g] = round(Int, gens[g, :OtherVarCost] + gens[g, :HeatRate] * fuel_price) end return costs end # The data file's variable costs are the 2022 ones @assert variable_costs(gas_price, coal_price) == gens.VarCost println("| Generator | Fixed cost (\\\$/MW-yr) | Variable cost (\\\$/MWh) |") println("|:--|--:|--:|") for g in 1:n_types println("| $(gens[g, :Plant]) | $(commas(gens[g, :FixedCost])) | $(gens[g, :VarCost]) |") end ``` | Generator | Fixed cost (\$/MW-yr) | Variable cost (\$/MWh) | |:--|--:|--:| | Nuclear | 790,000 | 8 | | Coal | 392,000 | 27 | | NG CCGT | 82,000 | 48 | | NG CT | 65,000 | 69 | ::: {.caption} Variable costs at 2022 fuel prices: gas \$7\.21, coal \$2\.36 per million Btu (MMBtu). ::: Demand: NYISO Zone C, every hour of 2020 (peak 2,781 MW). ::: {.notes} Fixed costs are annualized: the cost of building one MW of capacity, spread over the plant's life, per year. Variable costs are per MWh generated, and they are mostly fuel. The fuel prices are what U.S. power plants paid on average in 2022, when natural gas cost about twice the 2025 Henry Hub average. A CCGT burns about 6\.27 million Btu of gas per MWh and a CT about 9\.12, so every dollar on the gas price adds about 6 and 9 dollars to their costs per MWh. The last part of the lecture changes that price. Nuclear is very expensive to build and cheap to run; combustion turbines are the reverse. Wind, solar and geothermal come later. ::: ## Load Duration Curve ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} sorted_demand = sort(demand, rev=true) p_ldc = plot(1:n_hours, sorted_demand, color=:black, xlabel="Hours of the year with at least this load", ylabel="Load [MW]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 3000)) plot!(p_ldc, size=(1200, 360), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The year's hourly loads, sorted from highest to lowest, show **how many hours** each load level is reached. ::: {.notes} The chronological demand curve (one point per hour through the year) makes it hard to see how often each level occurs. Sorting turns it into a load duration curve: read any point as "the load is at least this high for this many hours". The top few hundred MW are needed only a handful of hours a year; the bottom 1,175 MW are needed every hour. ::: ## Decision Variables **What are the decision variables?** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} ::: {.small} | Variable | Meaning | |:--:|:-------------------| | $x_g$ | installed capacity (MW) of generator type $g \in \mathcal{G}$ | | $y_{g,t}$ | production (MWh) of type $g$ in hour $t \in \mathcal{T}$ | | $NSE_t$ | non-served energy (MWh) in hour $t$ | ::: **Do we have to meet demand in every hour?** ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} This might be cost-prohibitive. Instead, price **non-served energy** at some large penalty (here \$9,000/MWh). ::: ::: {.notes} Two kinds of decisions: how much to build (x, one per technology) and how to run it each hour (y, one per technology per hour). Non-served energy is load we choose not to serve; its cost stands in for the damage of a shortfall. ERCOT, the Texas grid operator, capped wholesale prices at 9,000 dollars per MWh until the end of 2021. ::: ## The Formulation **What are the objective and constraints?** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} ::: {.small-math} $$ \begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{NSE}} \quad & \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \text{FixedCost}_g \, x_g + \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \text{VarCost}_g \, y_{g,t} \\ & \quad + \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \text{NSECost} \, NSE_t \\[0.3em] \text{subject to:} \quad & \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} y_{g,t} + NSE_t \geq d_t \qquad \forall t \in \mathcal{T} \\[0.3em] & y_{g,t} \leq x_g \qquad \forall g \in \mathcal{G}, t \in \mathcal{T} \\[0.3em] & x_g, \, y_{g,t}, \, NSE_t \geq 0 \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Board item. Build the objective in two pieces: investment (fixed cost times capacity) and operation (variable cost times generation, plus the penalty on unserved energy). Constraints: each hour, generation plus unserved energy covers demand; no plant produces more than its installed capacity; everything is non-negative. Ask: is this an LP? Yes: it's linear in every variable, capacity is divisible (we model total MW, not individual units), and demand is treated as known. Mixed integer programming relaxes the second of these assumptions and stochastic programming the third. ::: # Interpreting the Solution ## Implementation in `JuMP` ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="false" code-line-numbers="|1|3-7|8-9|10-11|12"} NSECost = 9000 gencap = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) @variables(gencap, begin x[g in 1:n_types] >= 0 # capacity [MW] y[g in 1:n_types, t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # generation [MWh] NSE[t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # non-served energy [MWh] end) @objective(gencap, Min, sum(gens[g, :FixedCost] * x[g] for g in 1:n_types) + sum(gens[g, :VarCost] * y[g, t] for g in 1:n_types, t in 1:n_hours) + NSECost * sum(NSE)) @constraint(gencap, load[t in 1:n_hours], sum(y[:, t]) + NSE[t] >= demand[t]) @constraint(gencap, availability[g in 1:n_types, t in 1:n_hours], y[g, t] <= x[g]) set_silent(gencap); optimize!(gencap) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} 8,784 hours times four technologies is about 35,000 generation variables; HiGHS solves it in a few seconds. Naming the load constraint lets us read its shadow prices, the hourly prices, after the solve. ::: ## Utilization How much of the year is a plant's capacity used? $$\text{utilization} = \frac{\text{energy produced in the year}}{\text{capacity} \times \text{hours in the year}}$$ - A 100 MW plant that produced 219,600 MWh in 2020's 8,784 hours: 25% utilization. - Note that this simple capacity expansion model does not include the economic dispatch constraints. **What does this mean for the utilization values**? ::: {.notes} A plant that ran at full output all year would be at 100%, and one that never ran at zero. EIA calls this number the plant's capacity factor. Today we keep the term capacity factor for what the weather allows a wind or solar plant to produce, which comes later, and use utilization for what the model chooses to run. ::: ## Results ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} capacity = value.(x) generation = [sum(value.(y[g, :])) for g in 1:n_types] unserved = value.(NSE) nse_hours = count(unserved .> 1e-6) # Cost and emissions of this plan, to compare with the plans that follow thermal_cost = objective_value(gencap) # [$/yr] thermal_emissions = sum(gens[g, :Emissions] * generation[g] for g in 1:n_types) # [t CO₂/yr] # One decimal place, and plain 0 rather than -0.0 for technologies that aren't built function share(v) rounded_v = round(v; digits=1) if rounded_v == 0 return "0" end return string(rounded_v) end # Energy produced as a share of what the capacity could produce in a year [%]; # a dash for a type that isn't built function utilization(built, produced) if built < 0.5 return "–" end return string(round(Int, 100 * produced / (built * n_hours))) end println("| Resource | Installed (MW) | % of peak | Energy (GWh) | % of energy | Utilization (%) |") println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|") for g in 1:n_types println("| $(gens[g, :Plant]) | $(commas(capacity[g])) | $(share(100 * capacity[g] / peak_demand)) | ", "$(commas(generation[g] / 1000)) | $(share(100 * generation[g] / sum(demand))) | ", "$(utilization(capacity[g], generation[g])) |") end ``` | Resource | Installed (MW) | % of peak | Energy (GWh) | % of energy | Utilization (%) | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Nuclear | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | – | | Coal | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | – | | NG CCGT | 2,154 | 77.4 | 15,322 | 99.2 | 81 | | NG CT | 596 | 21.4 | 127 | 0.8 | 2 | Up to **31 MW** goes unserved, in **7 hours** of the year. ::: {.notes} No nuclear and no coal: neither is worth building at these costs. Combined-cycle gas carries almost all of the energy, and its utilization is 81%. Combustion turbines are 21% of peak demand but supply only 0\.8% of the energy: they're for the peaks. And there is some unserved energy, despite the 9,000 dollar penalty: 94 MWh over 7 hours. The total cost is \$960M a year. ::: ## Which Plant Serves Which Load? ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # One color per plant type, in the order of the data file type_colors = [cb_purple, :gray40, cb_orange, cb_vermillion, cb_blue, cb_sky, cb_yellow] # The load duration curve, filled by the plant type that serves each level of load. # Plants are used in order of running cost (`order`, cheapest first), so each type # fills a band as tall as its capacity. function band_plot(build, order) p = plot(xlabel="Hours of the year with at least this load", ylabel="Load [MW]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 3000), legend=:outerright) lower = zeros(n_hours) served = 0 for g in order if build[g] > 0.5 served += build[g] upper = min.(sorted_demand, served) plot!(p, 1:n_hours, upper, fillrange=lower, color=type_colors[g], linewidth=0, label=gens[g, :Plant]) lower = upper end end plot!(p, 1:n_hours, sorted_demand, fillrange=lower, color=:black, linewidth=0, label="Unserved") plot!(p, 1:n_hours, sorted_demand, color=:black, linewidth=2) return p end thermal_build = zeros(nrow(gens)) thermal_build[1:n_types] = capacity p_bands = band_plot(thermal_build, [1, 2, 3, 4]) plot!(p_bands, size=(1200, 330), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The CCGT band is full most of the year (utilization **81%**). The CT band is used only at the far left (**2%**). ::: {.notes} The load duration curve again, colored by the plant that serves each MW of load. The plants run in order of cost, so the CCGTs take every MW of load up to their capacity and the CTs take what is above it. The height of a band is that type's capacity and its area is its energy, so utilization is how much of its rectangle the band fills. The CCGT rectangle is mostly full. The CT rectangle is nearly empty: 596 MW that are used 2% of the time. The load at the far right, which is there in every hour, is called base load; the load at the far left, there for a few hours, is peak load. Here one type serves both the base and the middle. The unserved load is a sliver above the CTs at the left edge, too thin to see at this scale. ::: ## Screening Curves ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Annual cost of one MW of each technology, as a function of how many hours it runs hours_run = 0:n_hours annual_cost = zeros(length(hours_run), n_types + 1) for g in 1:n_types annual_cost[:, g] = gens[g, :FixedCost] .+ gens[g, :VarCost] .* hours_run end annual_cost[:, end] = NSECost .* hours_run # not serving: no build cost ct_vs_ccgt = (gens[3, :FixedCost] - gens[4, :FixedCost]) / (gens[4, :VarCost] - gens[3, :VarCost]) nse_vs_ct = gens[4, :FixedCost] / (NSECost - gens[4, :VarCost]) # The next slide's equations quote these four numbers @assert gens[3, :FixedCost] == 82000 && gens[3, :VarCost] == 48 @assert gens[4, :FixedCost] == 65000 && gens[4, :VarCost] == 69 p_screen = plot(xlabel="Hours run per year", ylabel="Cost per MW [\$1000/yr]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 900), legend=:outerright) for (j, (name, color, style)) in enumerate(zip([gens[1:n_types, :Plant]; "Unserved"], [cb_purple, :gray40, cb_orange, cb_vermillion, :black], [:solid, :dash, :solid, :dashdot, :dot])) plot!(p_screen, hours_run, annual_cost[:, j] ./ 1000, color=color, linestyle=style, label=name) end vline!(p_screen, [ct_vs_ccgt], color=:black, linewidth=1, linestyle=:dash, label=false) annotate!(p_screen, ct_vs_ccgt + 150, 720, text("$(commas(ct_vs_ccgt)) h", 16, :left, plot_font)) plot!(p_screen, size=(1200, 440), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Each line is what one MW of a technology costs per year if it runs for a given number of hours: fixed cost at zero hours, rising at the variable cost. The cheapest technology for a load that lasts h hours is the lowest line at h. At these prices nuclear and coal are not the lowest at any number of hours in a year. CTs are cheapest below the crossover with CCGT; CCGTs above. Unserved energy (the dotted line, steepest of all) is cheapest only for loads that last a few hours: its crossover with CTs is too close to zero to see at this scale. ::: # Adding Renewables ## What Changes With Renewables? Wind and solar are **intermittent** and can't produce at full capacity every hour: their **capacity factor** $c_{g,t}$ depends on the weather. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} The capacity constraint changes from $$y_{g,t} \leq x_g \qquad \text{to} \qquad y_{g,t} \leq x_g \times c_{g,t}$$ ::: ::: {.notes} For thermal plants, c is 1 in every hour. A MW of solar that produces at midday when load is low is worth less than one that produces at the evening peak. That's why screening curves don't apply to wind and solar: the value of a renewable MW depends on which hours it produces, not only on how many. ::: ## Where Capacity Factors Come From - Resource data: wind, sun, water or heat available each hour. - Often a **typical meteorological year (TMY)** or a few **actual meteorological years (AMY)**, sometimes only selected periods. - A TMY smooths out extremes, and a few AMYs sample only a few years. Both keep the problem small at the expense of simplifying meteorology. ::: {.notes} A typical meteorological year stitches together typical months from many years, which smooths out the extremes: the windless week, the cloudy month. Planning for a typical year can under-build for the bad ones. That is a structural choice in the model. ::: ## Wind and Solar Capacity Factors ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} profiles = DataFrame(CSV.File("data/capacity_expansion/wind_solar_capacity_factors.csv")) # The profiles cover a 365-day year and 2020 has 366 days, so February 28 is used again for February 29 before_leap_day = 1:(59 * 24) feb28 = (58 * 24 + 1):(59 * 24) after_leap_day = (59 * 24 + 1):nrow(profiles) wind_cf = [profiles.Wind[before_leap_day]; profiles.Wind[feb28]; profiles.Wind[after_leap_day]] solar_cf = [profiles.Solar[before_leap_day]; profiles.Solar[feb28]; profiles.Solar[after_leap_day]] wind_average = sum(wind_cf) / n_hours solar_average = sum(solar_cf) / n_hours # Average capacity factor in each hour of the day n_days = div(n_hours, 24) wind_by_hour = zeros(24) solar_by_hour = zeros(24) for h in 1:24 wind_by_hour[h] = sum(wind_cf[h:24:end]) / n_days solar_by_hour[h] = sum(solar_cf[h:24:end]) / n_days end p_profiles = plot(1:24, wind_by_hour, color=cb_sky, label="wind", xlabel="Hour of the day", ylabel="Average capacity factor", ylims=(0, 1), xticks=0:6:24, legend=:topleft) plot!(p_profiles, 1:24, solar_by_hour, color=cb_orange, linestyle=:dash, label="solar") plot!(p_profiles, size=(1200, 350), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: In this dataset, wind averages **34%** and solar **35%**. ::: {.notes} The figure averages each hour of the day over the whole year. Solar produces only in daylight and peaks at midday. Wind is steadier across the day and a little stronger at night. The two annual averages are close, but the hours of the day are very different. Since the profiles' source is not recorded, the plans in this lecture pair Zone C's load with wind and sun from an unknown site. ::: ## Geothermal, Wind and Solar ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} geothermal_row = n_types + 1 wind_row = n_types + 2 solar_row = n_types + 3 n_all = nrow(gens) # Average share of capacity that is available over the year, by type average_available = ones(n_all) average_available[wind_row] = wind_average average_available[solar_row] = solar_average println("::: {.small}\n") println("| Generator | Fixed cost (\\\$/MW-yr) | Variable cost (\\\$/MWh) | Average capacity factor (%) |") println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|") for g in (n_types + 1):n_all println("| $(gens[g, :Plant]) | $(commas(gens[g, :FixedCost])) | $(gens[g, :VarCost]) | ", "$(round(Int, 100 * average_available[g])) |") end println("\n:::") ``` ::: {.small} | Generator | Fixed cost (\$/MW-yr) | Variable cost (\$/MWh) | Average capacity factor (%) | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | Geothermal | 470,000 | 0 | 100 | | Wind | 91,000 | 0 | 34 | | Solar | 70,000 | 0 | 35 | ::: Geothermal is available in every hour, but only where the resource exists. ::: {.notes} None of the three has a fuel cost. Wind and solar are cheap to build and available only when the weather allows. Geothermal costs more to build than coal and runs whenever it is wanted. Its cost is the Energy Information Administration's estimate for a 50 MW plant. Real sites are small and need the right geology, so letting the model build as much as it wants is generous to geothermal. Because geothermal is always available, the screening rule still applies to it: it beats a CCGT for loads that last more than 8,083 hours a year. ::: ## Do Screening Curves Still Work? ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Wind and solar on the screening chart: a fixed cost each year, and nothing per MWh solar_vs_ct = (gens[solar_row, :FixedCost] - gens[4, :FixedCost]) / gens[4, :VarCost] wind_vs_ccgt = (gens[wind_row, :FixedCost] - gens[3, :FixedCost]) / gens[3, :VarCost] # What a MWh costs once the capacity factor is counted [$/MWh] wind_energy_cost = gens[wind_row, :FixedCost] / (wind_average * n_hours) solar_energy_cost = gens[solar_row, :FixedCost] / (solar_average * n_hours) geothermal_energy_cost = gens[geothermal_row, :FixedCost] / n_hours # A CCGT's whole cost per MWh when it runs all year [$/MWh] ccgt_all_year_cost = gens[3, :FixedCost] / n_hours + gens[3, :VarCost] p_renewable_screen = plot(xlabel="Hours run per year", ylabel="Cost per MW [\$1000/yr]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 520), legend=:outerright) plot!(p_renewable_screen, hours_run, annual_cost[:, 3] ./ 1000, color=cb_orange, label="NG CCGT") plot!(p_renewable_screen, hours_run, annual_cost[:, 4] ./ 1000, color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dashdot, label="NG CT") hline!(p_renewable_screen, [gens[wind_row, :FixedCost] / 1000], color=cb_sky, linestyle=:dash, label="Wind") hline!(p_renewable_screen, [gens[solar_row, :FixedCost] / 1000], color=cb_green, linestyle=:dot, label="Solar") plot!(p_renewable_screen, size=(1200, 370), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## The Cost of a Solar MWh A MW of solar costs \$70,000 a year and averages 35% of its capacity. What does a MWh cost? ::: {.fragment .fade-in} - Solar: 70,000 ÷ (0\.346 × 8,784 h) = **\$23/MWh** - Wind: 91,000 ÷ (0\.342 × 8,784 h) = **\$30/MWh** - CCGT fuel: **\$48/MWh** ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Both cost less than the gas they save, but neither is available at this capacity in every hour. ::: ## Adding Renewables in `JuMP` ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Share of each type's capacity that is available each hour: all of it for the # thermal types and geothermal, the capacity factor for wind and solar available = ones(n_all, n_hours) available[wind_row, :] = wind_cf available[solar_row, :] = solar_cf # The least-cost plan for the listed plant types, with an optional cap on annual # emissions [t CO₂]. Costs default to the data file's; pass others to change them. function solve_plan(types; cap=Inf, fixed_cost=gens.FixedCost, var_cost=gens.VarCost) model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) @variables(model, begin x[g in types] >= 0 # capacity [MW] y[g in types, t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # generation [MWh] nse[t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # non-served energy [MWh] end) @expression(model, emitted, sum(gens[g, :Emissions] * y[g, t] for g in types, t in 1:n_hours)) @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed_cost[g] * x[g] for g in types) + sum(var_cost[g] * y[g, t] for g in types, t in 1:n_hours) + NSECost * sum(nse)) @constraint(model, [t in 1:n_hours], sum(y[g, t] for g in types) + nse[t] >= demand[t]) @constraint(model, [g in types, t in 1:n_hours], y[g, t] <= x[g] * available[g, t]) if isfinite(cap) @constraint(model, emissions_cap, emitted <= cap) end set_silent(model) optimize!(model) build = zeros(n_all) # capacity by type [MW]; zero for types left out hourly = zeros(n_all, n_hours) # generation by type and hour [MWh] energy = zeros(n_all) # generation by type over the year [MWh] for g in types build[g] = value(x[g]) for t in 1:n_hours hourly[g, t] = value(y[g, t]) end energy[g] = sum(hourly[g, :]) end carbon_price = 0 if isfinite(cap) carbon_price = shadow_price(emissions_cap) end return (types=types, build=build, hourly=hourly, energy=energy, unserved=value.(nse), cost=objective_value(model), emissions=value(emitted), carbon_price=carbon_price) end ``` ::: ```julia @constraint(model, [g in types, t in 1:n_hours], y[g, t] <= x[g] * available[g, t]) ``` Only the availability constraint changes: `available[g, t]` is 1 for the thermal types and geothermal, and the capacity factor for wind and solar. ::: {.notes} The folded cell holds the whole model as a function, so the same code can be solved for any set of plant types, with or without an emissions cap, and later at other fuel prices. Everything in it is the model from earlier except this one line. Writing the constraint with indexed sets keeps it one line however many technologies there are. ::: ## Results With Renewables ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} with_renewables = solve_plan(1:n_all) # Totals of the whole-MW values the table shows, so the text and the table agree renewables_added = round(with_renewables.build[wind_row]) + round(with_renewables.build[solar_row]) gas_before = round(capacity[3]) + round(capacity[4]) gas_after = round(with_renewables.build[3]) + round(with_renewables.build[4]) # The notes say geothermal is not built @assert with_renewables.build[geothermal_row] < 0.5 # For the notes: the plan if geothermal were the only addition, and the plan at # higher wind and solar fixed costs [$/MW-yr] with_geothermal = solve_plan(1:geothermal_row) higher_renewable_cost = copy(gens.FixedCost) higher_renewable_cost[wind_row] = 153000 higher_renewable_cost[solar_row] = 141000 higher_renewable = solve_plan(1:n_all; fixed_cost=higher_renewable_cost) # Generation above demand in a plan [MWh/yr]. Plants that cost nothing to run could produce # more than the load (the excess would be curtailed); the tables report each type's output # as the energy it supplies, which holds while this stays below half a GWh function above_demand(plan) return sum(max.(vec(sum(plan.hourly; dims=1)) .+ plan.unserved .- demand, 0)) end @assert above_demand(with_renewables) < 500 # Energy each type supplies over the year [MWh]. Geothermal, wind and solar cost nothing to # run, and when some of their output isn't needed the model doesn't say which of them is # turned down, so each hour their combined output is split in proportion to what each could # have produced function supplied_energy(plan) energy = zeros(n_all) for g in plan.types if gens[g, :VarCost] > 0 energy[g] = plan.energy[g] end end for t in 1:n_hours produced = 0 could_produce = 0 for g in plan.types if gens[g, :VarCost] == 0 produced += plan.hourly[g, t] could_produce += plan.build[g] * available[g, t] end end if could_produce > 0 for g in plan.types if gens[g, :VarCost] == 0 energy[g] += produced * plan.build[g] * available[g, t] / could_produce end end end end return energy end renewables_energy = supplied_energy(with_renewables) println("::: {.small}\n") println("| | Thermal only (MW) | Thermal only (GWh) | With renewables (MW) | With renewables (GWh) |") println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|") for g in 1:n_all if g <= n_types before = commas(capacity[g]) before_energy = commas(generation[g] / 1000) built_before = capacity[g] else before = "–" before_energy = "–" built_before = 0 end if built_before > 0.5 || with_renewables.build[g] > 0.5 || g == geothermal_row println("| $(gens[g, :Plant]) | $(before) | $(before_energy) | $(commas(with_renewables.build[g])) | ", "$(commas(renewables_energy[g] / 1000)) |") end end println("| Cost (\\\$M/yr) | $(commas(thermal_cost / 1e6)) | | $(commas(with_renewables.cost / 1e6)) | |") println("| CO~2~ (kt/yr) | $(commas(thermal_emissions / 1000)) | | $(commas(with_renewables.emissions / 1000)) | |") println("\n:::") ``` ::: {.small} | | Thermal only (MW) | Thermal only (GWh) | With renewables (MW) | With renewables (GWh) | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | NG CCGT | 2,154 | 15,322 | 1,579 | 5,194 | | NG CT | 596 | 127 | 650 | 167 | | Geothermal | – | – | 0 | 0 | | Wind | – | – | 1,842 | 5,139 | | Solar | – | – | 1,817 | 4,950 | | Cost (\$M/yr) | 960 | | 729 | | | CO~2~ (kt/yr) | 6,659 | | 2,325 | | ::: Wind and solar add **3,659 MW**; gas falls by only **521 MW**. ::: {.notes} Three things change. Wind and solar are built: 3,659 MW between them. The gas plants run less: the CCGTs' utilization falls from 81% to 37%, which is where the saving of \$231M a year and the 65% cut in emissions come from. And the gas capacity falls much less, from 2,750 to 2,229 MW, because demand after dark still has to be met. Nuclear, coal and geothermal are not built. Halving that with thermal types only means building 880 MW of nuclear in place of CCGT, and the plan's cost goes from \$960M to \$1,275M a year. With renewables available the same cap changes nothing. The uncapped plan with wind and solar already emits only 35% of the thermal-only total, so the cap does not bind and its shadow price is zero. Tighter caps do bind. At 25% the plan adds wind, solar and a little geothermal. At 10% geothermal serves the base of the load, and the plan builds less wind and solar than at 25%, because a plant that is always available leaves fewer hours for them to fill. Nuclear is not built in any plan that can build geothermal, which costs less to build and nothing to run. Where there is no geothermal resource, nuclear is the alternative, and the 10% cap then costs \$570 a tonne against \$110. ::: ## Intuition About The CO~2~ Shadow Price Swap a MW of CCGT for nuclear, both running all year. Each plant's cost per MWh is its fixed cost spread over 2020's 8,784 hours, plus its variable cost: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} $$ \frac{\overbrace{\left(\underbrace{790{,}000 / 8{,}784}_{\text{fixed}} + \underbrace{8}_{\text{variable}}\right)}^{\text{nuclear, \$/MWh}} - \overbrace{\left(\underbrace{82{,}000 / 8{,}784}_{\text{fixed}} + \underbrace{48}_{\text{variable}}\right)}^{\text{CCGT, \$/MWh}}}{0.43 \text{ t/MWh}} $$ That is **\$94\.4 per tonne**, the thermal-only shadow price. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} This **carbon price** is the cost of abating the last tonne. With renewables it is **\$0** at this cap, **\$78** at 25% and **\$110** at 10%. ::: ::: {.notes} Board item. With thermal types only, the LP reported a shadow price of −\$94\.42 a tonne on the last slide. The shadow price is the value of one more tonne of allowed emissions, which is also the cost of abating the last tonne. With thermal types only there is one way to abate: replace a CCGT with a nuclear plant, both running all year, and the arithmetic gives the shadow price. With renewables there are cheaper ways to avoid a tonne, and at a 50% cap they are in the plan already, so the price is zero. The price rises as the cap tightens because the cheapest abatement is used first. ::: ## Natural Gas Prices Since 2019 ::: {#34 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} gas_history = DataFrame(CSV.File("data/capacity_expansion/gas_prices_monthly.csv"; types=Dict(:Month => String))) n_months = nrow(gas_history) # Position of each month on the time axis: January 2019 is 2019.0 month_position = zeros(n_months) for i in 1:n_months month_position[i] = 2019 + (i - That is the price at which coal's line on the screening chart meets the CCGT's at the end of the year. ::: # Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule ## Key Takeaways ::: {.incremental} - Capacity expansion chooses **what to build** and **how to run it** together, at least total cost. - With **screening curves**, we can read the least-cost thermal build off the load duration curve: each type serves the hours in which its total cost per MW is lowest. - The value of wind and solar depends on *when* they produce. - A **CO~2~ cap's shadow price is a carbon price**: the cost of abating the last tonne. - The plan depends on **fuel prices**: expensive gas moves the base load to other plants. ::: ## Next Classes **Wednesday, November 4**: Quiz 4, then mixed integer programming. **Monday, November 9**: Solid waste and network models. **Wednesday, November 11**: Lab 3, fixed costs and facility siting in `JuMP`. ## Assessments **Mini-Project 2**: Due Friday, November 20. **Homework 7**: Assigned Wednesday, due Thursday, November 12. **Quiz 4**: Wednesday, November 4. # Appendix ## A Week With Wind and Solar ::: {#38 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # The week around the year's peak hour, under the plan with renewables peak_hour = argmax(demand) week = max(1, peak_hour - 84):min(n_hours, peak_hour + 83) built = findall(with_renewables.build .> 0.5) week_mix = zeros(length(week), length(built) + 1) for (j, g) in enumerate(built) week_mix[:, j] = with_renewables.hourly[g, week] end week_mix[:, end] = with_renewables.unserved[week] areaplot(1:length(week), week_mix, label=permutedims([gens[built, :Plant];
